title: Transpose: swapping rows and columns

what.formal: The transpose of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$, written $A^{\mathsf T}$, is the $n \times m$ matrix whose $(i,j)$ entry is $A_{ji}$: every row becomes a column and every column becomes a row. A matrix is symmetric if $A = A^{\mathsf T}$, which requires it to be square.
what.plain: Turn the table on its side. What was a row is now a column, and nothing else changes.

what.md: **Transpose as a change of direction.** In card 1 the incidence matrix had rows for vertices and columns for hyperedges, and $H^{\mathsf T}x$ summed a per-vertex signal over each hyperedge. Transposing gives you the opposite traversal: paths that ran from vertices to edges now run from edges back to vertices. Equations that move information back and forth in a structure — which is what all of Equation (1) is — are built by alternating a matrix with its own transpose.

**Symmetry is the special case worth naming.** An adjacency matrix is symmetric because adjacency has no direction: if $i$ is adjacent to $j$, then $j$ is adjacent to $i$. Degree matrices are diagonal, hence symmetric. The Laplacian is symmetric. Almost everything in this subject is symmetric, and the interesting quantities (its eigenvalues) are exactly the ones that survive transposition.

example.md: **Example 1 — see it happen.** Take the incidence matrix of the four-person graph, which is $4 \times 3$:

example.note: Every column of $H$ has become a row of $H^{\mathsf T}$, so the shape goes from $4 \times 3$ to $3 \times 4$. Column $e_1$ of $H$, which read $(1,1,0,0)$, is now row 1 of $H^{\mathsf T}$ — **a hyperedge's membership list, laid out horizontally.**

gloss.md: the transpose — rows and columns exchanged
a $3 \times 3$ matrix; entry $(e, f)$ counts the vertices shared by hyperedges $e$ and $f$

items.md: Now multiply $H$ by its own transpose: $H H^{\mathsf T}$, which is $(4 \times 3)(3 \times 4) \to 4 \times 4$.
items.why: Shapes first. A square result tells you this matrix is about *pairs of vertices* — the same kind of object as an adjacency matrix.

items.md: Entry $(u,v)$ counts the hyperedges containing **both** $u$ and $v$: $H H^{\mathsf T} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.
items.why: Check the diagonal: entry $(2,2) = 3$ is the number of hyperedges containing vertex 2 — its degree. Off the diagonal, $(1,2) = 1$ because vertices 1 and 2 share exactly one edge.

items.md: Compare with $A + D$, where $A$ is the adjacency matrix and $D$ the degree matrix: $A + D = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.
items.why: They are identical. This is not a coincidence of the example: $H H^{\mathsf T}$ puts the degree on the diagonal and the number of shared edges off it, which for a plain graph is exactly $A + D$. **The incidence matrix and the adjacency matrix are two encodings of the same structure, related by a transpose.**

example.md: The identity $H H^{\mathsf T} = A + D$ holds for **plain graphs**, where every hyperedge has two members. On a true hypergraph it does not — and the difference is informative: $(u,v)$ becomes the number of *relationships* $u$ and $v$ share, which can exceed 1 in ways a plain graph cannot express.

quiz.q: What does transposing do to a $4 \times 3$ matrix?

opts.expl: The *values* are unchanged but their positions are not: entry $(2,1)$ moves to $(1,2)$. A transpose that changed nothing would be the identity, and only square symmetric matrices have that property.

opts.md: Produces a $3 \times 4$ matrix in which each column of the original is a row
opts.expl: Correct. This is why transposing an incidence matrix turns membership lists from vertical to horizontal, and why alternating $H$ with $H^{\mathsf T}$ moves information from vertices to edges and back.

opts.md: Produces a $3 \times 4$ matrix in which the entries are inverted
opts.expl: Transposition is a rearrangement, not an arithmetic operation on the values. In particular a 0 stays a 0.

quiz.q: For the four-person graph, what is entry $(2,2)$ of $H H^{\mathsf T}$?
quiz.hint: The diagonal entry $(v,v)$ counts the hyperedges containing $v$ — the same quantity card 2 of the graph-theory section named.
quiz.sol: Vertex 2 lies in all three edges, so the entry is 3. In general $(H H^{\mathsf T})_{vv}$ is the degree of $v$, because each 1 in row $v$ of $H$ multiplies itself once. This is why $H H^{\mathsf T} = A + D$ rather than $A$ alone — the diagonal has to carry the degrees.

quiz.q: Why do graph methods repeatedly alternate a matrix with its transpose?

opts.md: To keep the matrices square so they can be inverted
opts.expl: Invertibility is rarely the goal here; $H$ itself is not square and nobody inverts it.

opts.md: Because the two directions carry information in opposite senses — vertices to relations, then relations back to vertices
opts.expl: Correct. One pass collects each relation's membership into a summary; the transpose pass distributes that summary back to the members. Equation (1) is exactly this round trip, which is why it reads $H$ then $H^{\mathsf T}$ with a normalisation wedged between them.

opts.md: Because the transpose is cheaper to compute than the original
opts.expl: They cost the same; in most implementations the transpose is never materialised at all.

close: **Where this is going:** the paper's Equation (1) is a vertex → hyperedge → vertex round trip: $H$ sends each vertex's value into its relations, then $H^{\mathsf T}$ sends the relation summaries back out. Cards 3 and 4 supply the two remaining operations Equation (9) needs.
